seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Early July to early October, once the east-side snow is gone from the Scatter Lake basin and the south ridge scramble is dry

May.reason: Snow still fills the upper Scatter Creek trail and the talus above the lake, and the slopes above Scatter Lake can release wet-snow slides in warm spells.

June.reason: The lower trail melts out early on this dry east-side peak, but snow often lingers on the slope above Scatter Lake and on ledges around the ridge gendarmes.

July.reason: The route is generally snow-free by early July, water is still easy to find near the lake, and the class 3 gendarmes are dry; start early to beat the heat.

August.reason: Dry and snow-free, but the burned lower trail and sun-baked scree slope are hot, water above Scatter Lake is scarce, and wildfire smoke is common.

September.reason: Cooler days on the long scree slope, a dry ridge, and larches around Scatter Lake start to turn late in the month.

October.reason: Larches peak early in the month, but the first light snow can coat the ridge ledges and shorter days leave less margin on the loose descent.

evidence: WTA / Wenatchee Outdoors: route generally snow-free by early July; best May-Oct; larches above 6,400 ft (https://wenatcheeoutdoors.org/2017/01/20/scatter-lake-abernathy-peak/)
Oct 7 2021 trip: larches just past prime, light early snow near summit; trail passes burn zone; 1,200 ft scree treadmill (https://www.lucasmountainknowledge.com/post/abernathy-peak-oct-2021)
WTA TR Aug 2022 (https://www.wta.org/go-hiking/trip-reports/trip_report.2022-08-20.5769320288)
flags: Stored season Jun-Oct agrees; June kept as marginal because snow commonly lingers above the lake until early July.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late June through mid-September, once the Aasgard slope and base gully melt out and the wall's cracks have dried

May.reason: The Stuart Lake Trailhead road is often still snowbound and the slope above Colchuck Lake and the base gully hold avalanche-prone spring snow.

June.reason: In low-snow years the wall is dry by early June, but most years wet snow lingers on the Aasgard slope and seeps can keep the thin cracks wet.

July.reason: The approach slope and gully are melting out, snow patches in the gully still give water, and the west-facing wall is dry for sustained crack climbing.

August.reason: Reliably dry rock, but the wall takes full afternoon sun and gets hot on the 5.12 crux; the gully's snow patches may be gone, so carry water from the lake.

September.reason: Cooler temperatures suit hard free climbing, though mornings on the shaded wall are cold and a long car-to-car day runs into shorter daylight.

October.reason: Larch season crowds the trail, nights freeze and early storms can glaze the cracks; camping in the permit zone still needs the lottery permit.

evidence: Steph Abegg Let it Burn / West Face TRs: approach 400 ft up Aasgard then left through brush to gully (https://stephabegg.com/trip-reports/washington/cbr-let-it-burn/)

CascadeClimbers TR Let it Burn + West Face 6/6/2015 in a low-snow year; gully snow patches give water (https://cascadeclimbers.com/forum/topic/97521-tr-colchuck-balanced-rock-let-it-burn-and-west-face-662015/)
Row access: Enchantment overnight permit season May 15-Oct 31; row approach: Aasgard slope exposed to wet-snow slips into July
flags: Stored window Jul-Sep; evidence shows the route goes in early June of low-snow years, so June is marked marginal rather than out of season.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through early September, after the snow at the base of Burgundy's north side melts back and before fall cold sets in

May.reason: SR 20 has usually just reopened, the scree gullies to Burgundy Col are snow-loaded, and the route's base below the col is still buried.

June.reason: Snow eases the slog to the col but can be dangerous on the north side, the base traverse may need an axe, and the lichen-covered cracks are often wet.

July.reason: The approach melts out and water flows near the bench, but steep snow at the base can persist into midsummer; later July is better.

August.reason: The base traverse is mostly snow-free, the cracks are dry, and the north side stays cool; water near the col dwindles to a trickle.

September.reason: Stable weather and cool rock on the north side, though the loose gully below the col is bare scree and daylight is shorter.

October.reason: The shaded north side is cold, early snow can coat the col, and WSDOT typically closes SR 20 at Washington Pass as winter storms arrive.

evidence: SummitPost Burgundy Spire: best July-Sept; approach to col easier when snow covered but dangerous on the face (https://www.summitpost.org/burgundy-spire/151368)

Row approach: base scramble below north face may need an axe into midsummer; row access: SR 20 closed roughly mid-Nov to mid/late April
flags: Consistent with stored Jul-Sep window.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through August, once Agnes and Spruce Creeks drop and the col and gully still hold enough snow for the descent

June.reason: Agnes and Spruce Creeks run high with snowmelt over the only log crossings, and the approach basins above the creek are still snow-covered.

July.reason: Snow on the col and gully helps the couloir descent but adds route-finding and moats on the ridge; creek crossings on logs are still fast and cold.

August.reason: Lower creeks, a melted-out ridge crest and longer days for the 19-20 hour summit day; wildfire closures on the Agnes Creek corridor are possible.

September.reason: The gully is icier or bare and loose, days shorten on a route needing a headlamp, and fire closures on the PCT corridor have closed this approach before.

October.reason: The Stehekin shuttle season is winding down, early snow reaches the high camp, and daylight is too short for the long summit push.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July through September, when Nason Ridge is snow-free, the meadows bloom and Ninemile Saddle is dry

May.reason: Snow still covers the ridge and Ninemile Saddle, and south-facing slopes on the Merritt Lake side of Nason Ridge can avalanche in spring.

June.reason: One of the first high hikes in the area to melt out; the ridge is often snow-free by late June, though snow can linger at Ninemile Saddle early.

July.reason: Snow-free trail and peak wildflowers along the ridge; there is little reliable water, so carry enough for the whole hike on hot days.

August.reason: Wildflowers linger and the exposed saddle is dry, but the burned lower trail is hot and wildfire smoke or fire closures are possible.

September.reason: Cooler hiking and fall color on the ridge; water sources are driest now and blowdown across the burn area may slow the lower trail.

October.reason: Fall color persists, but early snow can cover the trail past the Nason Ridge junction and make it hard to follow, and the narrow saddle gets slick.

evidence: Hike of the week 2025: wildflowers throughout summer; FR 6910 unsigned turn, narrow rough spur (https://www.hikeoftheweek.com/2025/06/12/alpine-lookout/)

Mountaineers TRs: late June ridge snow-free; late Oct snow from Nason Ridge junction, lost trail, ~22 trees down in burn; early Oct 1/2 in snow (https://www.mountaineers.org/activities/trip-reports/alpine-lookout-round-mountain)
Row best_season: first high point on Nason Ridge to shed snow; flowers July-Aug; fall color Sept-Oct
flags: Consistent with stored Jun-Oct window.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through August, once Twin Lakes Road melts out and the face's 45-degree gully still holds firm snow

June.reason: The upper Twin Lakes Road and the approach are usually still snowbound, and the face's gullies hold avalanche-prone spring snow.

July.reason: Firm early-morning snow makes the glacier and the 45-degree gully straightforward, though in big years the road's last miles stay snowed in until late July.

August.reason: The approach is open, snow still fills the key gully for step-kicking, and the glacier is well bridged early in the month; loose rock above demands care.

September.reason: The gully can melt out to hardpacked, loose ground with nothing solid, moats widen at the glacier edge, and fall storms begin.

October.reason: Early snow and verglas on the upper face, a crevassed glacier and a rough, closing access road leave little margin.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through early September, when Upper Cathedral Lake is snow-free and the long Pasayten approach is dry

June.reason: The high basin around Upper Cathedral Lake often still holds snow, creeks run high, and the cold cracks on the buttress may be wet.

July.reason: The basin melts out and the rock dries, but mosquitoes peak along the approach and afternoon thunderstorms threaten a sustained 5.11 route.

August.reason: Dry cracks and fewer bugs; start early to finish the roofs before afternoon storms, and expect wildfire smoke or fire closures in the Pasayten.

September.reason: Stable weather early in the month, but nights near the lake freeze and cold hands on the ringlock crux slow a long route.

October.reason: The first snows arrive at Upper Cathedral Lake, the crack system stays cold, and the long walk out leaves little margin in a storm.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through early September, when Upper Cathedral Lake is snow-free and the buttress's cracks are dry

June.reason: Snow usually lingers around Upper Cathedral Lake and the short scramble to the buttress, and the opening chimney can stay wet.

July.reason: The lake basin melts out and the hand crack dries, but mosquitoes are worst along the approach and afternoon thunderstorms are common.

August.reason: Dry rock and a short approach from the lake camp make it easy to finish before afternoon storms; watch for wildfire smoke and fire closures.

September.reason: Climbed into early September; cold nights at the lake and loose upper pitches reward waiting for the sun to warm the rock.

October.reason: The first snows reach the 7,400 ft lake basin and the long Pasayten approach offers little margin if a storm arrives.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through early September, when the Upper Cathedral Lake basin is snow-free and the slab start is dry

June.reason: Snow often still covers the basin around Upper Cathedral Lake, and the steep opening slab with its thin crack may be wet from melt.

July.reason: The basin melts out and the rock dries, but July brings the worst mosquitoes on the approach and afternoon thunderstorms on a long route.

August.reason: Dry cracks and settled weather; start early so the slow third-pitch crux is done before afternoon storms, and check for Pasayten fire closures.

September.reason: Early September stays climbable, but freezing nights at the lake and shorter days add pressure on the crux pitch.

October.reason: Early snow reaches the high lake basin and the long approach offers little escape if a storm arrives.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August to mid-September, once the north-facing cracks have dried and before cold nights chill the shaded wall

June.reason: Snow still fills the Cathedral Lakes basin and the talus below the north wall, and the cracks on this shaded face run with meltwater.

July.reason: The approach melts out and the buttress dries, though early in the month snow patches linger at its base and the high creeks run full.

August.reason: Dry, warm rock on a face that sees little sun; the main risks are afternoon thunderstorms and wildfire smoke or closures in the Pasayten.

September.reason: Settled weather and cooler approach days; by late month the shaded north wall gets cold for the off-width finish and nights drop below freezing.

October.reason: The first snows of the season usually arrive at 8,000 ft, glazing the north face, and a two-day approach leaves little margin for a storm.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July to early September, once snow clears from Cathedral Pass and the ridge steps, before autumn snow returns

June.reason: Cathedral Pass and the north side of the ridge are still under snow, and the loose steps are wet or snow-plastered.

July.reason: The ridge is usually free of snow by mid-month; early July can still hold snow on the north-facing steps, and thunderstorms become frequent.

August.reason: Snow-free, dry rock on the whole ridge; start early to be off the exposed crest before afternoon storms, and watch for fire closures.

September.reason: Stable weather and fewer storms, but cold mornings on a north-facing line and the risk of an early dusting late in the month.

October.reason: Early snowfall at 8,000 ft makes the loose blocks and exposed steps treacherous, and the long approach is committing in unsettled weather.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July to early September, after the moat and gully at the base melt out and before the wall turns cold

June.reason: Firm snow fills the north-facing gully and moat at the base of the Ka'aba Buttress, and the approach basin is still snowbound.

July.reason: The cracks dry out, but the gully and moat at the base can hold hard snow into July; bring a way to deal with it early in the month.

August.reason: The base is snow-free and the crack pitches are dry; thunderstorms and wildfire smoke or closures are the main things that stop a trip.

September.reason: Early September is still prime, but the shaded buttress gets cold for hand cracks and the descent traverse can ice up after a storm.

October.reason: First snowfall usually reaches the buttress and descent traverse, and short days leave little room on a two-day approach.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July to August, after the approach basin melts out, choosing a window between fire closures and the first autumn snow

June.reason: Snow lingers in the approach basin and gullies into late June, and creek crossings on the long approach run high with snowmelt.

July.reason: The scree and grass slopes are mostly snow-free and creeks drop, making it a good time to go before the Pasayten fire restrictions set in.

August.reason: The most settled weather for this walk-up; seasonal fire restrictions, smoke and possible area closures are the thing to check.

September.reason: Stable days and quieter trails, but nights turn cold at the lakes and by late month an early snowfall can cover the talus.

October.reason: The first lasting snow usually arrives at this elevation, hiding loose talus and making the two-day approach committing.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late May to early June, while the couloir holds consolidated spring snow and the trailhead road has opened

April.reason: The trailhead road is usually still gated, adding miles of snowy walking, and the couloir can hold unconsolidated or avalanche-prone snow.

May.reason: The trailhead road typically opens in May and late-month freeze-thaw firms the 35-50 degree couloir; start early before the sun softens it.

June.reason: Early June still has continuous snow in the narrows; as the month goes on the couloir thins, ice shows at the constrictions and the exit gets wet.

July.reason: The couloir melts out into loose rock, brush and moats, rockfall increases in the narrow slot, and the Colchuck Glacier descent opens up.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July to mid-September, after the snow clears from the approach gully and while this shaded north side stays warm enough

June.reason: SR 20 is open, but the climbers' gully to the notch is usually snow-filled and can be icy until late June.

July.reason: The gully melts out and the north-side cracks dry; the loose gully is busy, so rockfall from parties above is the main hazard.

August.reason: Reliably dry granite and long days; a north aspect stays pleasant on hot days, though smoke from regional wildfires can hang over the pass.

September.reason: Stable weather and fewer parties in the gully, but the shaded north side gets cold and the first snow can dust the tower late in the month.

October.reason: Cold, short days and early snow on a north face; SR 20 closes for winter once the snow comes, often in November.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July to early August, while snow bridges still span the glaciers and the moat at the col is filled

June.reason: The Cascade River Road may still be gated below the trailhead, the approach is snowbound with avalanche risk, and the river crossing runs high.

July.reason: Continuous snow on the Inspiration, McAllister and Klawatti Glaciers keeps crevasses bridged and the col moat filled, easing the rappel.

August.reason: The summit tower is dry, but crevasses open fast on the long glacier traverse and the moat at the rappel point widens as the month goes on.

September.reason: Bare ice and open crevasses on all three glaciers lengthen the traverse, the col moat can be awkward to cross, and days shorten for a long outing.

October.reason: Early storms load thin snow bridges over open crevasses, and the Cascade River Road closes at the Eldorado gate for winter.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August to September, in a multi-day dry spell, when the vegetated gneiss has drained and snow is gone from the east side

June.reason: Snow lingers in the upper Barclay Creek drainage and east-side gullies, and the vegetated cracks still run with meltwater.

July.reason: The east-side slopes melt out and days are long enough for an exploratory line, but the rock needs several dry days after any rain.

August.reason: Usually the driest stretch on this maritime peak, so the vegetated ledges drain best; morning sun on the east face speeds drying.

September.reason: Vegetation is at its driest and thunderstorm cycles fade; watch for the first autumn rains that can soak the face for days.

October.reason: A clear spell can still be climbable, but short days and the first snow at summit level make an unrepeated line committing.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-August to mid-September, in a multi-day dry spell, after the couloirs below the wall melt out

July.reason: Snow clears from below the wall by mid-to-late July, but the north face needs several rain-free days before its seams dry.

August.reason: Usually the driest stretch on this maritime wall; the approach hillside dries out and long days suit a long, slow route.

September.reason: Vegetation on the ledges is driest and summer thunderstorm cycles fade; the first autumn rains can end the season abruptly.

October.reason: Short days on a north face that gets little sun, and once autumn rains start the wall goes wet and stays wet.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late August to late September, once the sandstone slab is fully dry and the long approach creeks are low

July.reason: The slab dries out as the snow above it melts, and lingering snow on the descent can make the loose Shovel Lake side easier.

August.reason: Dry, grippy sandstone and low creeks; the slab faces southeast and bakes by afternoon, and wildfire closures can shut the trailhead.

September.reason: Cooler days on a sunny slab and dry rock; check for fire closures in the Salmon La Sac area, which have shut the trailhead into autumn.

October.reason: Short days make an 11-12 mile approach plus 2,000 ft of slab tight, and the first autumn rain or snow ends the season.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July to mid-September, after the SW Face gullies and Dutch Miller Gap shed their early-summer snow

July.reason: Gully snow melts out through the month; late July usually gives dry Class 3-4 terrain, though the 15-mile approach is buggy.

June.reason: Snow still covers the high traverse between Chain Lakes, Doelle Lakes and Bullseye Pass, and the steep heather-and-talus slope below the summit.

July.reason: The south-facing granite dries early, but snowfields can linger on the north side of the passes and around Doelle Lakes into mid-July.

August.reason: The cross-country traverse is snow-free and the lakes make easy camps; watch for afternoon thunderstorms on the exposed one-person summit perch.

September.reason: Cooler, stable weather for the multi-day traverse and dry, grippy granite on the short roped pitches.

October.reason: Frost and early snow on the ridge crest make the sparsely protected crux and the down-climb off compact granite much riskier.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August, when the north ridge has finally shed most of its snow and verglas

June.reason: The northwest couloir is still a snow climb and the north ridge is snow-loaded, while the long North Fork Entiat approach is under snow near Saska Basin.

July.reason: The approach and Saska Basin melt out, but the north ridge often still holds enough snow to force a traverse onto the east face.

August.reason: The best chance of a dry north ridge; the couloir may be loose scree rather than snow, so an axe is still worth carrying.

September.reason: Stable weather, but the shaded ridge can pick up verglas after the first cold nights, and late-summer wildfire can close the approach.

October.reason: New snow and ice on the north side and short days make the ridge a poor choice; the south-side slopes are the usual fallback.

July.reason: The approach melts out and Challenger Glacier bridges are solid, but the Impasse may still hold steep snow and the water-polished gully can run wet.

August.reason: The only known ascent was in early August: dry gneiss on the lower buttress and a snow-free ridge, with high camps on Easy Peak.

September.reason: The rock stays dry, but the Challenger Glacier opens up and bare-ices, making the crossing to the buttress slower and more crevassed.

October.reason: Short days on a 2,000-ft route three days from the car, and early snow on the loose upper ridge and the Impasse.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late June to late July, when the north face has melted back but snow still eases the approach and upper slopes

May.reason: The north face is still plastered and the high approach is under deep, avalanche-prone snow; the Ross Lake water taxi has not yet started.

June.reason: The only known ascent came in late June, when the face had melted back enough to climb while snow still covered the high approach.

July.reason: The face is drier and the approach glacier and moraine are passable; the 400 ft of summit snow is still firm in the morning.

August.reason: Dry rock, but receding snow exposes more loose rubble above the face, and wildfire smoke or closures are common in the Pasayten.

September.reason: Cold, short days on a shaded north face and a bare, icy approach glacier; morning-sun rockfall stays a hazard on the lower pitches.

August.reason: Dry rock on the crux slab and a snow-free approach; afternoon thunderstorms build quickly over the Tatoosh.

September.reason: Cool, stable days on the southeast face and a fully clear scree traverse.

October.reason: The first snow and frost make the 5.8 slab and exposed scrambling slick, and Stevens Canyon Road closes once significant snow arrives.

September.reason: Fewer storms and cooler temperatures on the sunny south face, but cold nights at the lakes and the first snow can arrive late in the month.

October.reason: New snow and ice on the upper face and summit chasm, and a multi-day approach with no cell coverage in cold, short days.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July to mid-September, after the steep snowfield at the base of the buttress melts and the loose rock dries

July.reason: The trail to Cathedral Pass is clear, but a short, steep snowfield can remain at the start of the route through much of July.

August.reason: The base is snow-free and the fractured rock is dry; still expect loose blocks and rockfall throughout the six pitches.

September.reason: Cool, stable weather for a shaded northeast face and a dry, snow-free approach.

October.reason: The northeast aspect holds early snow and ice in its gullies, making the loose, poorly protected rock much more dangerous.

July.reason: Early July brings lingering snow on the approach and seeping rock on the northeast side; by late July it is usually climbable.

August.reason: The northeast ridge has had time to dry and the talus traverse is clear, though afternoon convection over the crest still builds.

September.reason: Cooler, more stable air and the driest rock of the year suit six marginal-protection pitches, with shorter days to watch.

August.reason: Snow-free approach and dry rock; loose blocks in the descent gully are the main hazard with other parties on nearby routes.

September.reason: Still dry and quieter, though shorter days and the first fall rain can make the loose rock and descent gully slick.

October.reason: Fall storms bring rain and early snow to the basin, and wet, loose rock makes the descent gully treacherous.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late August to September, when the Chiwawa River ford runs low and the Napeequa valley and Pilz Glacier edge are mostly snow-free

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late April to May and again in October, when temperatures are mild on this shadeless slope and spring wildflowers bloom

March.reason: Walk-in access is discouraged through March 31 to protect wintering mule deer, so plan the hike for April onward.

April.reason: The deer closure ends and the grassy slopes green up, with balsamroot starting late in the month; the road can be muddy after rain.

May.reason: Peak balsamroot and lupine bloom and moderate temperatures on the open slope make this the best month.

June.reason: Still pleasant early, but heat builds quickly on the shadeless slope; start early in the morning.

July.reason: Hot afternoons with no shade and intense UV; go at dawn with plenty of water or choose another month.

August.reason: Similar heat on an exposed slope, plus wildfire smoke that often hangs over the Chelan valley.

September.reason: Temperatures ease and the smoke usually clears late in the month, making the climb comfortable again.

October.reason: Cool, dry weather and clear views of Lake Chelan; the exposed slope is at its most comfortable.

evidence: Late April-May balsamroot peak; summer very hot, no shade https://www.wta.org/go-hiking/hikes/chelan-butte ; https://www.ordinary-adventures.com/2022/06/hiking-to-elephant-head-chelan-butte-trail/

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through August, after snow clears from the peak's southwest side and before autumn rains return to the Olympics

October.reason: Autumn rain returns to the Quinault and wet rock plus short days make the unpublished off-trail line hard to justify.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July, while snow still bridges the moat and the glacier icefall below the face is easy to pass

August.reason: The icefall opens and may need a short pitch of hard glacier ice, and the moat at the base of the face widens.

September.reason: Bare glacier ice, open crevasses and a wide, deep moat make reaching the rock slow and much more serious.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July through August, when the gully between the spires has melted out and the loose upper chimneys are dry

May.reason: Once SR 20 reopens in spring the basin and gully are still buried in snow, making this a snow climb rather than a rock route.

September.reason: Still in shape, though the shaded chockstone gully can hold ice after cold nights and days are shorter.

October.reason: Early snow and ice return to the shaded gully and SR 20 approaches its winter closure, which usually comes in November or December.
